title: Fintech, AI and the Future of Finance
excerpt: . Fintech, AI and the Future of Finance: How Intelligent Technology Is Transforming the Financial Industry. Artificial intelligence and financial technology are reshaping banking, lending, digital payments, investment management and financial risk assessment. As India accelerates its digital transformation, the convergence of fintech and AI is creating new opportunities for businesses, financial institutions and consumers while redefining the future of financial services. Introduction: Finance Enters the Age of Intelligence. The financial services industry is experiencing a fundamental shift. What once depended heavily on paperwork, manual verification and traditional banking infrastructure is increasingly driven by digital platforms, real-time data and intelligent automation. Financial technology, commonly known as fintech, has already changed how people transfer money, apply for loans, purchase insurance and manage investments. Artificial intelligence (AI) is taking this transformation further by enabling financial institutions to analyse complex information, automate decisions and deliver more personalised services. The combination of fintech and AI is creating a new generation of financial services that can be faster, more responsive and more data-driven. Banks are using AI to strengthen fraud detection, fintech companies are applying machine learning to credit assessment, and investment platforms are exploring intelligent tools to support portfolio analysis. In India, this transformation is supported by digital infrastructure such as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), electronic customer verification, digital banking and consent-based financial data sharing. However, the future of finance will not be determined by technology alone. Data privacy, cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, responsible AI and customer trust will play equally important roles in determining how successfully these innovations are adopted. 1. AI-Powered Banking: From Transactions to Intelligent Services. Traditional banking has largely focused on processing transactions, maintaining accounts and delivering standardised financial products. AI is enabling banks to expand these functions through intelligent customer support, predictive analytics and automated workflows. AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants can answer routine questions, explain transaction details, provide account-related assistance and guide customers through basic banking processes. Machine learning systems can also analyse customer interactions and transaction patterns to help identify service issues or detect potentially suspicious activity. For banks, these applications can improve operational efficiency and reduce the time employees spend on repetitive tasks. Customers may benefit from quicker responses and more convenient access to routine services. The next stage of AI-powered banking may involve more personalised financial assistance, including spending insights, savings guidance and proactive notifications about unusual account activity. Nevertheless, banks must ensure that AI systems provide accurate information, protect sensitive data and escalate complex or high-risk matters to qualified human personnel. 2. Intelligent Digital Payments and Fraud Prevention. Digital payments have become an essential part of India’s financial ecosystem. UPI, mobile banking and QR-code payments have made electronic transactions accessible to consumers and businesses across a wide range of settings. As transaction volumes grow, financial institutions face the challenge of detecting fraudulent activity without creating unnecessary barriers for legitimate users. AI can help address this challenge by analysing transaction patterns, device information, behavioural signals and other permitted data to identify unusual activity. title: AI applications in the banking industry: Automation is necessary, but strict control is required.
excerpt: . AI applications in the banking industry: Automation is necessary, but strict control is required. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly applied in banking operations, contributing to improved service quality but also posing inherent risks. To build protective barriers, the State Bank of Vietnam has issued Circular No. 53/2026/TT-NHNN regulating safety, risk management, and implementation conditions for the application of AI systems in the banking sector. Hà Nội Mới • 11/10/2026. AI is deeply involved in banking operations. According to statistics from the State Bank of Vietnam, by the end of 2025, nearly 89% of people aged 15 and above will have payment accounts; many credit institutions will have a rate of transactions through digital channels exceeding 95%. In the first six months of 2026, the number of cashless payment transactions increased by 34. 28%, and the value increased by 12. 24% compared to the same period last year. Many banks have applied AI, shifting from a support tool to increasingly participating in financial activities, from data analysis and personalized services to fraud detection and risk management. At Vietnam Foreign Trade Commercial Bank ( Vietcombank ), starting in August 2026, the bank launched the One Data Platform (ODP) project. This platform is geared towards providing advanced reporting and analysis services and laying the foundation for AI and machine learning applications. Meanwhile, at Tien Phong Commercial Joint Stock Bank (TPBank), AI is combined with big data and real-time analytics systems to identify abnormal behavior patterns early. TPBank CEO Nguyen Hung said the bank applies big data and AI to regularly monitor transactions, identify unusual behavior, detect risky transactions, and create safety barriers before risks become losses. The integration of AI into behavioral analysis and transaction control demonstrates that this technology is becoming more deeply involved in stages that directly impact the security of customer assets. This also provides a basis for clearer demands on risk management, monitoring, and the ability of humans to intervene. Maintain control. You may also like. Speaking at the "Digital Transformation Day for the Banking Industry 2026" event held on August 18th, Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Pham Duc An emphasized: "The deeper the digital transformation, the faster new issues related to institutions, data, cybersecurity, digital fraud, privacy protection, and artificial intelligence governance will emerge. This requires the banking industry to continue to innovate strongly, but with focus, control, and with tangible results as the measure. ". In this context, on September 30, 2026, the State Bank of Vietnam issued Circular No. 53/2026/TT-NHNN. The Circular takes effect from November 15, 2026, except for the provisions under Clauses 2, 3, and 4 of this regulation. The Circular stipulates safety, risk management, and implementation conditions for the application of AI systems in the banking sector. Notably, the Circular stipulates the classification of AI systems according to risk levels, identifying several cases as high-risk, such as AI systems that automatically execute payment transactions exceeding certain thresholds or automatically decide to grant credit of 50 million VND or more. For payment transactions, the risk threshold is determined based on both the value of each transaction and the total value of transactions for the day. For AI-powered automated payment transactions, customers and the service provider must have a prior agreement specifying the scope of transactions, transaction limits, daily limits, deadlines, and terms and conditions. Customers have the right to terminate the agreement and must have tools to proactively suspend or cancel the AI's authorization for automated payments. title: AI’s Value In Wealth Management Starts With Better Processes
excerpt: . Send to a colleague --> Print (subject to copyright) Request Reprint Rights. This article draws on interviews carried out for WealthBriefing's forthcoming AI in Wealth Management research report, due for publication later this year. For boutique wealth managers, the immediate opportunity of artificial intelligence lies in reducing administrative work and creating more capacity for client service. This article is part of conversations in a research report this news organisation is producing in partnership with Arta Finance. Arta Finance is an AI-driven wealth and fintech firm headquartered in Silicon Valley and Singapore. Its rapid ascent reflects how technology is reshaping the wealth management sector worldwide. The success of AI in wealth management may depend less on which tools firms buy than on how well they prepare their businesses to use them. That is the view of Kevin Andrews (main picture), chief operating officer at Bentley Reid , who has contributed to WealthBriefing’s forthcoming AI in Wealth Management research report. His responses highlight a shift from exploring the technology’s capabilities to establishing how it can deliver practical value within a regulated business. “12 months ago, we were largely exploring what AI could do. Currently we are focused more on how it can be used safely and practically within the business,” Andrews said. Bentley Reid has introduced an AI policy and governance on its use, with staff using tools such as Copilot for research, summarization, drafting and everyday productivity tasks. The firm does not allow AI to make investment decisions or generate client advice. For Andrews, the most significant change has been moving the discussion towards the business processes and data that support the technology. Creating capacity for client service Asked where AI could make the biggest difference to the economics of wealth management, Andrews points to productivity. Relationship managers spend considerable time preparing for meetings, writing reports, documenting conversations and finding information. Reducing that workload could give them more time for activities that benefit clients. “As a boutique wealth manager, we remain a people business. The real opportunity for us is helping our staff serve clients more effectively and consistently, while creating additional capacity as the business grows. ”. However, demonstrating a promising use case is only the first step. Turning it into something reliable, controlled and supported within daily operations requires a stronger business case. “It’s largely about proving that the value is real and repeatable,” Andrews said. A useful test is whether staff are still using a tool six months after its introduction because it continues to make their jobs easier. Adoption depends on everyday usefulness Some of the most effective applications Bentley Reid has found so far are straightforward: summarizing information, preparing first drafts, extracting meeting actions and helping structure documents. “They aren't particularly glamorous, but they save time and solve real problems,” Andrews said. Training helps staff understand both the capabilities and limitations of AI. But adoption ultimately depends on a tangible benefit. A tool that saves time has a clearer route into everyday use than one that adds another login or process. Data presents another challenge. Bentley Reid has a mixture of established and newer systems, with information held across different platforms. Making that information structured, accessible and understood is a priority alongside identifying practical applications. Human accountability remains central Bentley Reid’s measured approach also reflects the need to balance opportunities with appropriate controls. “Our starting point is that responsibility remains with the individual, not the AI,” Andrews said. HSBC Holdings PLC (LON: HSBA) is reportedly planning sweeping job reductions across its UK wealth management operation as the bank increases its use of artificial intelligence and digitally enabled services. Around 70% of financial adviser roles could be removed , while half of management and specialist positions are expected to go, according to the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the plans. The bank is understood to be conducting a consultation process , with affected employees potentially leaving by the end of October. HSBC does not publish a separate headcount for its UK wealth operation, although the business is thought to employ hundreds of relationship managers across the country. The proposed restructuring forms part of a broader efficiency drive led by chief executive Georges Elhedery , who has made greater use of AI a central part of HSBC’s strategy since taking charge in 2024. Elhedery has previously said generative AI would eliminate some roles while increasing productivity and enabling employees to deliver faster and more personalised services to customers. The scale of the reported reductions is particularly notable because HSBC had previously been expanding its UK wealth operations as part of efforts to grow assets under management. The bank has not confirmed the percentages reported by the FT or provided a financial target for the restructuring. The bank said:. HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider. We’re continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally enabled products and journeys to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers. For investors, the potential attraction is a material reduction in staffing costs and greater operating leverage if technology allows HSBC to service wealthy customers with fewer advisers. The risk is whether a sharply reduced advisory workforce can maintain the level of personalised service expected by higher-value clients, particularly in a business where relationships and individual advice remain important. The immediate questions are therefore how many roles ultimately disappear, what cost savings HSBC expects from the restructuring, and whether increased use of AI can improve productivity without damaging client retention or wealth-management growth. title: AI Agents are emerging as greater Cyber Threats to South Korea’s Banking Sector
excerpt: CYBER THREATS & ATTACKS. South Korea is facing growing concerns over a new generation of cyberattacks in which artificial intelligence could play an increasingly important role. Reports of attacks targeting financial institutions have raised questions about how AI-powered tools may be changing the speed, scale, and sophistication of cybercrime. Over the past several weeks, multiple financial institutions in South Korea have reportedly experienced cyber incidents, ranging from service disruptions to suspected data breaches. The incidents have increased concerns among customers and regulators, particularly because financial institutions hold highly sensitive information, including personal identification details, account information, and transaction records. Speaking at a cabinet meeting, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung reportedly highlighted the growing cybersecurity risks associated with artificial intelligence. The discussion comes at a time when governments and technology companies around the world are attempting to understand how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI systems could be misused for malicious purposes. One reported incident involved an AI-assisted system allegedly identifying vulnerabilities in a website providing loan-related services. According to reports, information belonging to 25,000 customers was subsequently compromised. Such incidents demonstrate the potential danger of combining automated vulnerability discovery with traditional hacking techniques. Significance of AI in cybercrime lies largely in its ability to automate tasks that previously required considerable technical expertise. AI systems can potentially scan websites, identify weaknesses, generate malicious code, analyze stolen information, and adapt their strategies much faster than a human attacker working alone. This does not necessarily mean that AI can independently conduct every stage of a sophisticated cyberattack, but it can significantly lower the technical barrier for individuals seeking to exploit digital systems. The development has therefore created a difficult challenge for banks and financial regulators. Security teams must not only defend against conventional hackers but also prepare for attacks in which automated tools can operate continuously and respond rapidly to defensive measures. At the same time, claims about AI agents independently carrying out major cyberattacks need to be examined carefully. Determining whether an attack was genuinely conducted by an autonomous AI agent, or by humans using AI-assisted tools, requires detailed forensic investigation. The distinction is important because AI can be used as a tool by attackers without being the primary decision-maker behind an operation. The broader international technology industry is also confronting similar concerns. AI developers have acknowledged that increasingly capable models can create new cybersecurity risks if their capabilities are misused. Governments, cybersecurity researchers, and technology companies are consequently increasing efforts to monitor the behavior of advanced AI systems and establish safeguards against malicious applications. Incidents being reported in South Korea illustrate a broader transformation in cybersecurity. As AI becomes more capable, cyberattacks could become faster, more automated, and potentially more accessible to less-skilled attackers. Financial institutions will therefore need to strengthen their defenses, improve real-time monitoring, and invest in systems capable of detecting AI-assisted attacks. Ultimately, the emergence of AI in cybersecurity is a double-edged development. The same technology that can potentially help attackers identify vulnerabilities can also help banks detect threats, protect customers, and respond to incidents.
